content.heading: 7.3 Constrained Optimization
content.paragraph: Engineers, economists, scientists, and mathematicians often need to find the maximum or minimum value of a quadratic form $Q(\textbf{x})$ for $\textbf{x}$ in some specified set. Typically, the problem can be arranged so that $\textbf{x}$ varies over the set of unit vectors. This constrained optimization problem has an interesting and elegant solution. Example 6 and the discussion in Section 7.5 will illustrate how such problems arise in practice.
The requirement that a vector $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ be a unit vector can be stated in several equivalent ways:

The expanded version (1) of $\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x} = 1$ is commonly used in applications.
When a quadratic form $Q$ has no cross-product terms, it is easy to find the maximum and minimum of $Q(\textbf{x})$ for $\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x} = 1$.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the maximum and minimum values of $Q(\textbf{x}) = 9x_{1}^{2} + 4x_{2}^{2} + 3x_{3}^{2}$ subject to the constraint $\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x} = 1$.

content.paragraph: It is easy to see in Example 1 that the matrix of the quadratic form $Q$ has eigenvalues $9$, $4$, and $3$ and that the greatest and least eigenvalues equal, respectively, the (constrained) maximum and minimum of $Q(\textbf{x})$. The same holds true for any quadratic form, as we shall see.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$, and let $Q(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ for $\textbf{x}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{2}$. Figure 1 displays the graph of $Q$. Figure 2 shows only the portion of the graph inside a cylinder; the intersection of the cylinder with the surface is the set of points $(x_{1},x_{2},z)$ such that $z = Q(x_{1},x_{2})$ and $x_{1}^{2} + x_{2}^{2} = 1$. The “heights” of these points are the constrained values of $Q(\textbf{x})$. Geometrically, the constrained optimization problem is to locate the highest and lowest points on the intersection curve.

image.alt: A three dimensional graph shows an elliptic paraboloid projecting a unit circle on a plane.
A three dimensional graph shows the cylindrical coordinates on an elliptic paraboloid in the form of an infinity sign.

example.paragraph: The two highest points on the curve are $7$ units above the $x_{1}x_{2}\text{-plane}$, occurring where $x_{1} = 0$ and $x_{2} = \pm 1$. These points correspond to the eigenvalue $7$ of $A$ and the eigenvectors $\textbf{x} = (0,1)$ and $- \textbf{x} = (0, - 1)$. Similarly, the two lowest points on the curve are $3$ units above the $x_{1}x_{2}\text{-plane}$. They correspond to the eigenvalue $3$ and the eigenvectors $(1,0)$ and $( - 1,0)$.

content.paragraph: Every point on the intersection curve in Figure 2 has a $z\text{-coordinate}$ between $3$ and $7$, and for any number $t$ between $3$ and $7$, there is a unit vector $\textbf{x}$ such that $Q(\textbf{x}) = t$. In other words, the set of all possible values of $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$, for $\text{∥}\textbf{x}\text{∥} = 1$, is the closed interval $3 \leq t \leq 7$.

It can be shown that for any symmetric matrix $A$, the set of all possible values of $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$, for $\text{∥}\textbf{x}\text{∥} = 1$, is a closed interval on the real axis. note.title: Theorem 6
note.heading: Theorem 6
note.paragraph: Let $A$ be a symmetric matrix, and define $m$ and $M$ as in (2). Then $M$ is the greatest eigenvalue $\text{λ}_{1}$ of $A$ and $m$ is the least eigenvalue of $A$. The value of $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ is $M$ when $\textbf{x}$ is a unit eigenvector $\textbf{u}_{1}$ corresponding to $M$. The value of $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ is $m$ when $\textbf{x}$ is a unit eigenvector corresponding to $m$.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the maximum value of $9x_{1}^{2} + 4x_{2}^{2} + 3x_{3}^{2}$ subject to the constraints $\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x} = 1$ and $\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{u}_{1} = 0$, where $\textbf{u}_{1} = (1,0,0)$. Note that $\textbf{u}_{1}$ is a unit eigenvector corresponding to the greatest eigenvalue $\text{λ} = 9$ of the matrix of the quadratic form.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: If the coordinates of $\textbf{x}$ are $x_{1}$, $x_{2}$, $x_{3}$, then the constraint $\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{u}_{1} = 0$ means simply that $x_{1} = 0$. For such a unit vector, $x_{2}^{2} + x_{3}^{2} = 1$, and

Thus the constrained maximum of the quadratic form does not exceed $4$. And this value is attained for $\textbf{x} = (0,1,0)$, which is an eigenvector for the second greatest eigenvalue of the matrix of the quadratic form.

content.paragraph: The next theorem generalizes Theorem 7 and, together with Theorem 6, gives a useful characterization of all the eigenvalues of $A$. The proof is omitted.

note.paragraph: Let $A$ be a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix with an orthogonal diagonalization $A = {PDP}^{- 1}$, where the entries on the diagonal of $D$ are arranged so that $\text{λ}_{1} \geq \text{λ}_{2} \geq \cdots \geq \text{λ}_{n}$ and where the columns of $P$ are corresponding unit eigenvectors $\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{n}$. example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: During the next year, a county government is planning to repair $x$ hundred miles of public roads and bridges and to improve $y$ hundred acres of parks and recreation areas. The county must decide how to allocate its resources (funds, equipment, labor, etc.) between these two projects. If it is more cost effective to work simultaneously on both projects rather than on only one, then $x$ and $y$ might satisfy a constraint such as

See Figure 3. Each point $(x,y)$ in the shaded feasible set represents a possible public works schedule for the year. The points on the constraint curve, $4x^{2} + 9y^{2} = 36$, use the maximum amounts of resources available.

example.paragraph: In choosing its public works schedule, the county wants to consider the opinions of the county residents. To measure the value, or utility, that the residents would assign to the various work schedules $(x,y)$, economists sometimes use a function such as

The set of points $(x,y)$ at which $q(x,y)$ is a constant is called an indifference curve. Three such curves are shown in Figure 4. Points along an indifference curve correspond to alternatives that county residents as a group would find equally valuable.2﻿ Find the public works schedule that maximizes the utility function $q$.

figure.caption: The optimum public works schedule is (2.1,1.4)
